question: According to reports, the ruling party of Türkiye (AKP) has opened a representative office in occupied Nicosia, in a historic building that is purportedly a cultural heritage monument, without the required permits and without a clear legal framework for the operation of foreign political parties in the occupied areas.

This development raises concerns about Türkiye’s growing political and administrative influence in the occupied areas of the Republic of Cyprus, as well as about the protection of cultural heritage and respect for the sovereignty of an EU Member State. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission agree that the operation of an office of the ruling party of Türkiye in the occupied areas constitutes further political and administrative interference in the territory of an EU Member State, and does the Commission intend to make a statement or take diplomatic action in relation to this?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to monitor and protect cultural heritage monuments in the occupied areas, especially in cases of the possible unauthorised use of listed buildings?
Does the Commission intend to raise the issue in the context of Euro-Turkish relations, calling on Türkiye to respect the relevant UN resolutions and the sovereignty of the Republic of Cyprus?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.10.2026) The Commission is aware of the news report regarding the matter raised by the Honourable Member of the European Parliament. It notes that the building in question is a listed building and private property. Türkiye is expected to respect international law, good neighbourly relations and the sovereignty of Member States.

The Commission has reiterated, including through bilateral contacts with the Turkish authorities, that the EU remains fully committed to a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue within the UN framework, in accordance with all relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in line with the principles on which the EU is founded and its acquis.

The Commission expects Türkiye to foster an environment conducive to the resumption of settlement talks under the UN’s auspices. The Commission has also consistently stressed the importance of protecting sites of cultural significance.

In that regard, since 2012, the EU has provided EUR 35 million in funding to the bicommunal Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage (TCCH) in Cyprus, covering around 80% of its budget. This funding derives from the EU Aid Programme for the Turkish Cypriot community. Thanks to EU support, the TCCH has been able to restore or protect over 200 cultural and religious monuments across Cyprus.
